title: Juicy: The Fried Chicken Story
summary: Josh and Chuck explore fried chicken as Chuck's favorite food. They cover fried chicken's disputed origins (Scottish frying traced by some food historians, with enslaved Black women in the American South perfecting the spicing), its role in Southern life and the railroad "waiter carriers" who sold it through train windows, Gordonsville, Virginia's fried chicken reputation, and the racist use of fried chicken stereotypes such as the Coon Chicken Inn and Birth of a Nation. They discuss the rise of chicken consumption and factory farming, pressure frying, Harland Sanders and KFC (including the Colonel impersonator story, the sale to Heublein and the trademark jokes), Popeyes' founding, KFC's popularity in China, Japan and Korea, Korean double-fried chicken, Nashville hot chicken, the chicken sandwich wars sparked by Chick-fil-A, and the science of brining and frying. The episode ends with a listener mail from Mike L. about urban planning and show requests.

segments.title: Chuck's favorite food and fried chicken favorites
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as Chuck's favorite food edition and they swap favorite fried chicken spots and styles, including Kroger, Publix, Watershed, and Opal Bryant's skillet-fried chicken.

segments.title: Origins: Scotland and the American South
segments.summary: They discuss fried chicken's roots, including 18th-century recipes and the theory that Scots taught enslaved people to fry chicken, with enslaved Black women in the South perfecting the spicing. They note West African braising traditions as an alternative theory.

segments.title: Fried chicken as a treat and Black women's entrepreneurship
segments.summary: Fried chicken was labor-intensive and a special-occasion food; enslaved families raised chickens. After emancipation, Black women sold fried chicken, and waiter carriers sold it through train windows, with Gordonsville, Virginia noted as a hub. Scholar Psyche Williams-Forston's work is mentioned.
topics: Building Houses out of Chicken Legs

segments.title: Racist fried chicken imagery and stereotypes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how Black women's fried chicken was appropriated and how racist caricatures, including a Salt Lake City chain logo and Birth of a Nation, were used to demean Black people. They tie this to the Watermelon episode.

segments.title: Chicken farming, pressure frying and Harland Sanders
segments.summary: Chicken consumption rose from 1960 to 2019 as factory farming made chicken cheap. Pressure frying allowed faster fast-food cooking. Harland Sanders started serving chicken at his Corbin, Kentucky service station and cafe, developed his recipe, and became Colonel Sanders.

segments.title: KFC, the Colonel's persona and Popeyes
segments.summary: They discuss Colonel Sanders' persona and reputation, a story about a driver spotting an actor who played the Colonel in ads, the sale of KFC and its renaming to KFC, the Colonel's later restaurant and lawsuit, and his family's response to Papa John's. They then cover Popeyes' founding in Louisiana and its name origin.

segments.title: Fried chicken around the world
segments.summary: KFC is especially popular in China, where it is the largest fast-food chain by store count, and is a Christmas tradition in Japan. Korean fried chicken is double-fried with a sticky glaze, and Korea had many fried chicken restaurants after the 1997 financial crisis, with steamed chicken before American occupation.

segments.title: Nashville hot chicken and chicken and waffles
segments.summary: They discuss Nashville hot chicken and its origin with Thornton Prince III in Hadley Park, the heat and greasiness, and moderation. They then turn to chicken and waffles, its link to the South and to New York and Los Angeles, and Gladys Knight's restaurant.
topics: Gladys Knight's House of Chicken and Waffles

segments.title: Chicken sandwich wars
segments.summary: They discuss the chicken sandwich wars sparked by Chick-fil-A's claim to have invented the chicken sandwich, the earlier chicken sandwiches of the 1930s, and the fast food chains that launched sandwiches around 2019 along with the reasons for the trend.

segments.title: Brining science and listener mail
segments.summary: They explain how brining and oil choice affect fried chicken, plus equipment tips. The episode ends with a listener mail from Mike L. about urban planning and show requests, followed by the sign-off.
